1.Nf3 d5 2.c4.name: Réti Opening
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4.background: According to Réti, the opening entered master play early in 1923, and Hans Kmoch called the system of attack Réti used against Rubinstein at Karlovy Vary 1923 the Réti Opening or Réti System. In modern usage the name refers only to Nf3 and c4 by White against ...d5, with at least one bishop fianchettoed and no early d4.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 e6.strategy: Defends d5 with a pawn and opens the f8-bishop, aiming for a solid set-up with pawns on d5 and e6. The cost is the c8-bishop, shut in behind e6 until a later pawn move gives it play. The game is solid, and White decides whether to fight for the centre or to fianchetto.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 c6.strategy: Holds d5 with the c-pawn and, unlike ...e6, keeps the c8-bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain. The cost is that the pawn takes c6 from the b8-knight, which usually has to go to d7. A solid game follows, in which Black gives up little.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4.name: Réti Opening: Advance Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4.background: Together with 2...dxc4, one of the two main independent lines of the Réti Opening. It keeps the game closed, and the structure resembles a Benoni Defence with the colours reversed: as Black does in the Benoni, White usually fianchettoes the kingside bishop.
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4.strategy: Gains space and keeps the position closed: the pawn takes c3 and e3 from White, so 3.Nc3 would lose a knight to ...dxc3. The cost is that an advanced pawn needs support and becomes a target once White attacks it with the f3-knight and a pawn on e3. Expect a closed, manoeuvring game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4.name: Réti Opening: Réti Accepted
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4.background: Together with 2...d4, one of the two main independent lines of the Réti Opening, the one that opens the game. The many ways White has to regain the pawn limit its popularity.
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once and leaves White to choose how to win it back, and there are many good ways. Black is behind in development, so cannot hope to hold the extra pawn: 3...b5?! is dubious because of 4.a4. Black must finish developing quickly and give the pawn back when needed, and the game opens up.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and adds a defender to d5, but after 3.cxd5 Nxd5 White has the central pawn majority and can gain time against the knight. Black still keeps a choice of solid set-ups.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and presses on d4 and e5, but nothing supports d5: 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 attacks the queen with a gain of time, and the knight on c6 has taken the c-pawn's natural support square.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 but leaves d5 to 3.cxd5. Recapturing with the queen lets 4.Nc3 gain a tempo, so Black does better to recapture with the knight, and then White gains central space against it. Playable, but White is the one with the initiative.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 but leaves d5 to the queen alone. After 3.cxd5 the recapture 3...Qxd5 runs into 4.Nc3 with a gain of time, while recapturing with the knight lets White gain the centre against it. Playable, but slower than the main replies.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 b5.name: Réti Opening: Zilbermints Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for nothing: 3.cxb5 simply wins a pawn, and after 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the knight attacks both the queen and the b5-pawn. Black has no development or open line to show for it.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for open lines, but 3.Nxe5 simply takes it, and Black has only some activity to show for the pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for d5. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is attacked with a gain of time, and White gets a full centre with Black's development behind.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Be6.strategy: Defends d5 with a piece and develops, so the pawn holds for now, but the bishop blocks the e-pawn and leaves b7 undefended. After 3.cxd5 Bxd5 4.Nc3 it is attacked again, so Black loses a tempo and White gets the easier game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Bf5.strategy: Develops outside the pawn chain and eyes b1, but leaves both b7 and d5 short of defenders: 3.Qb3 attacks b7 with cxd5 to follow, and Black struggles to keep both pawns.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop against the f3-knight, but with only the e2-pawn behind it the knight is not pinned, and b7 is left undefended. 3.cxd5 Bxf3 4.exf3 Qxd5 5.Nc3 drives the queen away with tempo and leaves White the bishop pair, and 3.Qb3 hits b7 at once.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Qd7.strategy: Blocks the c8-bishop, takes d7 from the b8-knight and loses time. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is attacked again, so Black has moved it twice while White develops and takes the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early and develops nothing. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 it is attacked again, and White develops with tempo and builds a big centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: A rim knight that can reach f5 but does not guard d5. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is attacked with a gain of time, and White gets a full centre while Black's pieces are still at home.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 a6.strategy: A slow move that does nothing for d5 or development; 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 wins a tempo and White takes the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 a5.strategy: Stops b4 but does nothing about d5 or development; 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains a tempo and White takes the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 but leaves d5 with only the queen to defend it. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is attacked with a gain of time, and the bishop has not yet come out to help.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the knight and weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal, without doing anything for d5. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 White gains a tempo and a lead in the centre that Black has not paid for.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 with the f-pawn but weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and e6 and does nothing for d5; 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains a tempo.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 h6.strategy: A slow pawn move that does not defend d5 or develop anything; 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains a tempo.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 h5.strategy: Wastes a move and weakens g5 and g6 while d5 is left to 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3, which gains a tempo.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5 and shuts in the c8-bishop, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn that no black piece can retake at once. White can hold it while Black regroups.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5 and takes d7 from the b8-knight, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn that no black piece can retake at once. The bishop on d7 is passive, and even after Black develops the knight, White holds the pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Bh3.strategy: The bishop is attacked by the g2-pawn and has no support, so 3.gxh3 wins a piece for nothing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn that no black piece can retake at once. The king stays in the centre with nothing in return.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: 3.Nxg5 wins it, as nothing defends g5, and h7 and f7 come under fire, while Black has weakened the kingside for nothing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3.strategy: The solid way to question the advanced pawn: White challenges it at once, and Black must support the pawn or trade it off. White keeps a flexible set-up in which pieces, not pawns, contest the centre, at the price of a slower start.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.b4.strategy: The sharper try: White throws a wing pawn forward to gain queenside space and open the long diagonal, so that a bishop on b2 can attack the d4 pawn. White is ready to give up a pawn for open lines and quick development, and Black's centre pawn becomes the target.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.Rg1.name: Réti Opening: Penguin Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.Rg1.strategy: Gives up castling on the kingside for a rook move that prepares a kingside pawn push, while the centre is left alone. It costs a tempo, leaves the king in the middle and lets Black, who already has more space, finish development undisturbed.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.b4 c5.name: Réti Opening: Advance Variation, Michel Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.b4 c5.strategy: The principled reply: the pawn attacks b4 and gives d4 a second support, so White has to settle the tension on the queenside at once. Black keeps the space advantage in the centre and answers a flank attack with a central pawn chain.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.b4 g5.name: Réti Opening: Advance Variation, Navara Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.b4 g5.strategy: A counter-gambit on the wing: if White takes on g5, ...e5 opens the f8-bishop against b4 and Black wins a pawn back. Sound, but it loosens the kingside, and White can simply keep developing instead of taking.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.b4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and keeps ...c5 in reserve, but leaves the b4 pawn unchallenged for the moment. White completes the fianchetto with Bb2, which attacks d4 at once, and Black has to defend the pawn with ...c5 anyway. Sound, but it hands White the choice of how to continue.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3 c5.strategy: Supports the d4 pawn with a pawn and keeps the space gained, so Black does not have to trade it. The cost is a more fixed structure: White now attacks the base of the chain from the flank, and Black must be ready for the pawn sacrifice that follows.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3 Nc6.strategy: Defends the advanced pawn with a piece and develops at the same time. If White takes on d4, Black recaptures with the knight, trades knights and brings the queen to the centre, with an open game and easy development. The cost is that no pawn backs the d4 pawn, so it stays under pressure.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3 dxe3.strategy: Gives up the advanced pawn and the space it won. If White recaptures with the d-pawn, Black can trade queens with check and cost White the right to castle; if with the f-pawn, the queens stay on and Black has developed nothing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3 c5 4.b4.name: Réti Opening: Reversed Blumenfeld Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3 c5 4.b4.strategy: The critical test of Black's set-up: White offers a pawn to open lines against the centre. If Black takes on e3 and then b4, White recaptures with a broad pawn centre and fast development, and the extra pawn on b4 is weak. White is generally thought to have enough compensation.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3 c5 4.a3.strategy: Prepares the b4 break in a quieter way: after b4 and ...cxb4 the a-pawn recaptures, so White keeps the e3 pawn instead of sacrificing it. The price is a tempo, which Black can use to consolidate the d4 pawn, and the pressure builds more slowly.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 d4 3.e3 c5 4.exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once and opens the e-file against Black's e-pawn. After ...cxd4 Black keeps the space in the centre and has a half-open c-file against the c4 pawn. A calm choice that gives up the tension and the critical test of Black's set-up.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3.strategy: The standard way to win the pawn back: the bishop is freed to take on c4, and Black is left somewhat undeveloped. White gets a small edge in an open game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Na3.strategy: Heads for c4 to win the pawn back with a developing move, leaving the central pawns free to decide on later. The knight is on the rim for a move and Black gains some time, but the extra pawn is hard to hold.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.Qa4+.strategy: Checks and recovers the c4 pawn on the next move with the queen. White wins the pawn back quickly without committing a central pawn, at the price of bringing the queen out early while Black simply goes on developing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e4.strategy: Takes space in the centre first and wins the pawn back with the f1-bishop, which already eyes c4. White gets a broad centre, but the pawn on e4 is a target: ...Nf6 attacks it at once, and White has to defend or advance it.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Be6.name: Réti Opening: Réti Gambit, Keres Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Be6.strategy: Holds the extra pawn with a developing move instead of weakening the queenside with ...b5. It is playable but not the most natural development, and the bishop can be hit by Ng5, so Black may lose time keeping the pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 e6.strategy: The natural reply: Black opens the f8-bishop and prepares to castle, giving the pawn back in return for easy development and a share in the centre. White's bishop takes on c4, but Black challenges the centre with a pawn and has a comfortable game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and holds back White's e-pawn, whose advance to e4 would be hit at once. Black accepts losing the c4 pawn but keeps the e-pawn flexible and develops towards castling.
